newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says N. Korea not promised specific aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says N. Korea not promised specific aid.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday insisted it never promised North Korea a specific amount of food aid in return for Pyongyang's participation in a briefing on proposed Korean peninsula peace talks.
But it sent another strong signal that additional U.S. food aid may soon be made available.

North Korea's ambassador to the United Nations, in an interview with CNN on Tuesday, charged that the briefing had twice been delayed because Washington had not carried through on its promise to provide the food aid.

But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters: "The United States never promised a specific amount of food aid to the North Koreans as an inducement to convince them to come to the table and have a briefing on the four-party talks."

"Perhaps -- and I mean this quite sincerely -- perhaps something was missed in the translation or just missed in the communication ... We did not promise to deliver food or to guarantee commercial shipments of food," he said.
The United States did approve an application for a private American grain company, Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc., for a license to export grain to North Korea.

But those negotiations have been bogged down over financing for the deal and the adminstration has refused to become involved in what it has called "commercial transactions" between North Korea and Cargill.

However, Burns stressed again on Wednesday that "we have been assiduous in listening to the (U.N.) World Food Programme and the other nonprofit organisations. When they have come forward with emergency appeals for grain to North Korea, the United States has responded."
He said the World Food Programme is considering another appeal and "we would look very seriously at that appeal."
Burns argued that despite Pyongyang's charges the United States "has acted in good faith...We've been quite straightforward with the North Koreans ... on what we can do and what we can't do."

Cargill, the largest privately held company in the United States and one of the world's biggest grain trading firms, received permission from the administration early last month to ship 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to the food-strapped communist nation.

Since then, the company has been trying to arrange the financing of the deal, but the issue appears to have become embroiled in the larger question of more food aid to the struggling country and in plans for U.S. officials to meet with North Korea on proposed peace talks with South Korea.
The diplomatic meetings have been scheduled twice in New York, but were postponed each time by North Korea, which said it first wanted to conclude grain talks with Cargill.
North Korea has tried to pressure the United States to help finance the grain deal, hoping Washington might be more willing to help if it meant the diplomatic talks would proceed.
But no further dates will be set for the talks, Burns said on Tuesday, until the U.S. side is confident that the North Koreans will actually attend the meetings.
